known_gap: No check in the product reads a passive's VALUE. The architecture is the same one F-0008 (reversed_diode) and F-S0-0001 (swapped_pins) name, and this case isolates a different consequence of it: compile_board calls verify_board(board, netlist) with the SAME netlist it just compiled from, so the verifier can answer 'is this board what I was told to build' but never 'is what we were told to build right' — and here the thing we were told to build is a capacitor that is ten times too small. Everything the verifier does read is geometry (III.1 connectivity, III.2 shorts, III.3/III.4 the pin-to-net map, II.1-II.3 placement, IV.1 land patterns) or a pinout (IV.2). A value is in neither. The gap has three separate faces, and all three were measured: (1) NO CHECK READS A VALUE. data/parts.py::capacitor() is the authority on a tabulated passive's figures, and it is keyed on the Samsung CL series (CL05B104KO5NNNC = 100nF, CL05B103KB5NNNC = 10nF). The KEMET K-series part numbers this board uses are in neither that table nor component_db.json, so capacitor('K103K15X7RF53H5') and capacitor('K104K15X7RF53H5') both return None — the product cannot read the value of its own capacitor off its own part number. This is the same data gap as F-0005 (every land pattern carries verified: false), stated in a different place: the drawing knows the part number and no figure. (2) THE REQUIREMENT IS WRITTEN DOWN AND READ BY NOBODY. component_constraints.py carries decoupling_cap_nf: 100 for the MAX485 and MAX3485; a repository-wide grep finds the key defined twice and consumed nowhere. (3) THE SECOND SOURCE CANNOT REACH IT. IV.2, the check that compares a part's pinout against the KiCad symbol, reports 'no part could be compared' for K103K15X7RF53H5 — and equally for the correct K104K15X7RF53H5, so closing the symbol lookup would NOT close this case. A symbol describes a part's TERMINALS; it says nothing about how many farads a capacitor holds.
expected_detector: NONE TODAY — this is a named false pass
description: C1, the ATmega's bypass capacitor, carries 10 nF where the design asks for 100 nF. The part is a KEMET ceramic disc: K104K15X7RF53H5 in the base (the EIA value code 104 = 100 000 pF = 100 nF) and K103K15X7RF53H5 in the defective board (103 = 10 000 pF = 10 nF). Same package, same X7R dielectric, same ±10% tolerance, same through-hole radial footprint at 5.08 mm pitch — the board is copper-for-copper identical, with the same two pads, the same tracks, the same vias and all 12 required connections routed. Only the part soldered into those two pads is wrong, and it is wrong by a factor of ten. The physics: a bypass capacitor supplies the fast edges the rail's trace inductance cannot, and it filters the rail; its impedance on the rail is 1/(2·pi·f·C), so at the tens of kHz to MHz of switching noise a 100 nF X7R presents a few ohms and a 10 nF presents ten times that. The consequence is not a dead board but a QUIET one: the ATmega's supply now rings and droops on every digital edge, outside the ATmega328P's own 4.75-5.25 V operating window, and the board works on an open bench and fails in the enclosure next to a relay, a long DHT22 cable or a switching supply. That is why the class is not critical: a wrong pinout or a reversed diode kills the board every time; a wrong bypass value works most of the time and fails under conditions nobody writes down.
seed_target: C1's part number and value in the NETLIST — a value defect, not a copper defect, so the netlist is the right place to seed it. The base netlist is backend/pcb_engine/netlist_dht22.json with C1's part number stated (K104K15X7RF53H5) and its value added (100nF), because the hand-written fixture names the part but not its value; the design intent for 100 nF is generators/arduino_parts.py::decoupling(), which emits value='100nF'. It ships as netlist.json. The seed changes C1 to mpn K103K15X7RF53H5 and value 10nF, and that ships as netlist_defective.json — both are here because this is a netlist-level defect: the calibration harness judges each board against the netlist it was compiled from, so a defect that lives in the netlist has to ship both. The defective board is recompiled from the defective netlist by the product's own compile_board, so the board carries the fault the way the product would emit it. THE ARTIFACT THAT CARRIES THE FAULT, and how a reader detects it: the BOARD, in C1's attrs. board_base.json says C1.attrs = {package: RADIAL-2, mpn: K104K15X7RF53H5, value: 100nF}; board_defective.json says C1.attrs = {package: RADIAL-2, mpn: K103K15X7RF53H5, value: 10nF}. Everything else is byte-identical — tracks equal, vias equal, pads equal, placement equal. In the full product the same number also reaches the BOM, because PcbNetlistGenerator copies comp.value onto the netlist component and the BOM compiler copies comp.value onto the row, so a BOM read against the requirement is where the fault is most legible to a person. Note what the board does NOT carry: the rendered SVG prints neither the value nor the MPN, and the 3D scene carries the MPN but not the value string, so an engineer looking at the picture sees nothing wrong; an engineer reading the board IR sees it in one line.
notes: THIS CASE IS A NAMED FALSE PASS AS OF 2026-10-21, and that is the finding, not a gap in the seed. Measured: the product's own verifier returns ok=True on the defective board and the gate says {emit: true, reason: '8 check(s) unproven (unknown rung)'}. NOTHING flips — no check changes status between the base board and the defective one, and the defective board judged against the DESIGN INTENT netlist also fails nothing. The base board is clean on every decidable check (II.1, II.2, II.3, III.1, III.1c, III.1d, III.2, III.3, III.4, III.4d, IV.1 all pass), so the difference is the defect and nothing else. The board-level twin seed(board_base) returns exactly the board that seed_netlist + compile_board produces — byte for byte — because from_netlist copies the netlist's part number and value onto the component's attrs and changes nothing else; the mutator's own run checks that equality and fails if it ever stops holding. The case is deliberately NOT critical: a wrong bypass value produces a board that works most of the time and fails under conditions nobody writes down, which is a much quieter failure than the dead board a wrong pinout produces, and a calibration set that called it critical would be claiming more than the physics supports. Fixing it needs the two things the other three false passes need and one more: a value authority that covers the parts the product actually chooses (a parts table keyed on the KEMET K series, or a rule that reads the EIA value code out of the part number), a check that compares a passive's value against the requirement (decoupling_cap_nf: 100 exists and is read by nobody), and a design intent that survives into the verifier.
